title: Anthropic bans users from abusive or cruel behavior towards Claude
content:
Anthropic has barred users from exhibiting “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” toward its models, as the company’s leaders continue to ponder machine consciousness.
The Verge first reported the change in policy.
A spokesperson for Anthropic, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, did not immediately respond to an inquiry about what could be considered “abusive or cruel”.
In an online user policy, the San Francisco-based company noted that its ban would not apply to common user frustrations, model testing or “dark creative themes”.
Anthropic’s usage policy previously contained restrictions on abusive conduct.
The company’s large language models have the ability to end a conversation if a user is being persistently harmful. When that feature rolled out last August, the company framed it as a safeguard for AI’s welfare.
“We remain highly uncertain about the potential moral status of Claude and other LLMs, now or in the future. However, we take the issue seriously, and alongside our research program we’re working to identify and implement low-cost interventions to mitigate risks to model welfare, in case such welfare is possible. Allowing models to end or exit potentially distressing interactions is one such intervention,” according to its website.
The notion of AI systems being conscious has been highly polarizing in and outside the tech world.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has said he cannot rule out the possibility.
Meanwhile, Sam Altman, CEO of rival OpenAI, has appeared averse to the idea.
“I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue,” he wrote in an X post, days after the New York Times reported on Anthropic leaders’ extensive conversations with religious scholars.

report.summary: Anthropic's updated usage policy bars 'sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior' toward Claude, citing uncertainty about model welfare and consciousness.
report.background: Anthropic has updated its usage policy to prohibit sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward Claude, as first reported by The Verge. The change extends earlier restrictions on abusive conduct and arrives amid growing internal and public debate over whether large language models could have moral status. Since last August, Claude has had the ability to end conversations when users are persistently harmful—a feature Anthropic framed as a safeguard for AI welfare. The company says it remains highly uncertain about Claude's potential moral status but takes the issue seriously. CEO Dario Amodei has said he cannot rule out model consciousness, while OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has warned against ascribing religious force or surrendering human judgment to AI. Anthropic's leaders have also held extensive conversations with religious scholars. The policy does not define what counts as abusive or cruel.
key_points: Anthropic now bans 'sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior' toward Claude. The company says the rule targets persistent harm, not ordinary user frustration, model testing, or dark creative themes. A spokesperson did not immediately clarify what specifically counts as abusive or cruel, leaving enforcement boundaries unclear.

The policy builds on an existing safeguard: Claude can end conversations when a user is persistently harmful. Anthropic rolled out that feature last August and described it as a low-cost intervention to mitigate risks to model welfare, in case models have some moral status.

The update reflects Anthropic's public uncertainty about AI consciousness. CEO Dario Amodei says he cannot rule out the possibility, and the company has consulted religious scholars. Rival OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has pushed back, calling the ascription of religious force to AI models a safety issue.

The change is polarizing because it blends user conduct rules with speculative AI welfare. It could set a precedent for how AI companies police human-AI interaction, but critics may see it as anthropomorphism, unclear censorship, or a distraction from concrete safety and alignment problems.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Anthropic's move signals that model welfare and user conduct are becoming formal policy areas, not just philosophical debates. Other labs may face pressure to define acceptable treatment of AI assistants, potentially adding abuse detection, conversation termination, and welfare reviews to product design. Developers building on Claude or similar models may need clearer UX for frustrated users, moderation pipelines, and logs to distinguish testing from abuse. For regular users, the practical effect may be modest—venting is still allowed—but Claude may end or refuse interactions it deems cruel. The bigger impact is cultural: it normalizes the idea that AI models deserve protection, while raising unresolved questions about anthropomorphism, free expression, and who defines cruelty.
report.tools: To follow the policy, read Anthropic's Usage Policy and its model welfare research page, and observe Claude's conversation-ending behavior in practice. For testing boundaries, open-source LLM red-teaming tools such as Garak and Promptfoo can probe refusal and moderation triggers. AI welfare evaluation efforts, including Eleos AI Research's work, offer context on how labs assess model sentience claims. Watch whether Anthropic publishes clearer enforcement criteria.
